prize_parts.citation: For the prediction of flat electronic bands at a magic twist angle in bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene

statement.case_for: I keep magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene (B038) with MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero and Bistritzer, and the exchange has strengthened rather than weakened my reasons. The core is unchanged: the Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model gave a quantitative prediction (flat bands at a specific twist angle) and nature then supplied correlated insulators and superconductivity in exactly that regime, a result that was not guaranteed. What the round added is that no member disputes the observation itself, that independent groups reproduced it and carried it to other moire platforms, and that six of eight files converged on the identical three names, which suggests the credit is not an artefact of any one member's framing. I would anchor the citation only on the two decisive, checkable items, the 2011 flat-band prediction and the 2018 observation of correlated and superconducting states, and deliberately claim no pairing mechanism, as Pearce and Johansson also propose. Answering the chair's question: I would still support the same configuration if the mechanism proved conventional, because the discovery is the new tunable regime and the observed phases, not the explanation. My preferred configuration has not changed from round 1; what changed is that I am now more explicit that the citation, not the credited set, is where the age and mechanism worries must be handled.
statement.case_against: The objections I take most seriously are unchanged and I do not think the exchange removed them. First, the field is about eight years old and the phase diagram is still being rewritten (fractional Chern states, competing pictures of superconductivity), so a prize now honours a platform and a set of observations more than a settled physical picture; waiting a few years would be defensible, as Lindroth argues. Second, the three-name cap forces an unfair omission: Yuan Cao as first author of the 2018 papers, the earlier twisted-bilayer theory of Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto, and other moire groups. The chair notes that several of us rely on recalled priority history, and I record that my claim that Bistritzer-MacDonald is the decisive quantitative prediction, and that the early theory did not fix the magic angle in the same way, is from memory and not verified in the supplied files. Third, if the committee judged that the mechanism matters, B045 is the cleanest fallback.

responses.point: Kroll argues that the invention-versus-discovery objection does not separate B038 from B045, since magic-wavelength trapping was also a prediction that nature allowed, and the 1e-18 systematics are a measured result; he would not oppose B038 but asks the citation for B045 to say what is specific to lattices versus ion clocks.
responses.response: This is a fair correction to my round-1 framing and I withdraw the sharper form of 'engineering, not discovery'. Katori's idea is a real physical insight and the independent confirmation at 1e-18 is the strongest maturity evidence on the whole shortlist. Where I still differ is breadth and what a second look at the evidence shows: lattice clocks have so far delivered much better accuracy and tests of constants and relativity that are consistent with existing theory, whereas twisted bilayer graphene delivered a phase of matter nobody was expecting from a continuum calculation. That is a weighting judgement, not a scientific defect in the clocks, and I would put B045 firmly as my first alternative. Your point that the ion clocks reach similar uncertainties is the one I would insist on in any B045 citation; I would also note that the redefinition of the second has not occurred and should not be treated as evidence of merit.

responses.point: Lindroth holds B045 first, argues the attribution is the cleanest and the physics stable, and says the weakness of B038 is maturity: seven to eight years, a changing field, and twist-angle disorder that makes quantitative comparison between laboratories harder than for clocks.
responses.response: The comparison-between-laboratories point is the best argument against my position and I give it real weight; a 1e-18 agreement between institutes is a standard of reproducibility that no moire experiment can match. But I would distinguish quantitative metrology from qualitative reproducibility: the existence of correlated insulators and superconductivity near the magic angle is not a sample-specific claim, since many groups on several platforms see it, and disorder affects the details of the phase diagram rather than whether the phases exist. On your question of what new physics the clocks have revealed, I would say the many-body effects in lattice clocks are interesting, but to date the tests of relativity and constants have been confirmations. I still prefer B038 on discovery content, but I accept that a committee that weights maturity and attribution above breadth could reasonably go your way, and I would not regard B045 as a poor outcome.

responses.point: Mehlig supports B038, adds 'which opened the field of moire quantum materials' to the citation, argues the Bistritzer-MacDonald paper is the decisive prediction because it fixed the magic angle quantitatively, and says waiting for the pairing mechanism would tie recognition to a question that may stay open for decades.
responses.response: I agree with the mechanism argument and with treating Bistritzer-MacDonald as the decisive prediction. On the wording, I would be cautious about adding 'opened the field of moire quantum materials' as a causal claim in the citation, because it implicitly credits all later moire work to the three named people and sharpens the objection from the omitted groups. I would keep the citation strictly to the prediction and the observation, and let the committee's longer text describe the field. On the other point, I share your sense that topological insulators (B023, B040) are deep and mature, but the chair's summary shows two competing credited sets and I do not see a defensible three-name resolution this year, so I would not move toward them.

responses.point: Olsson supports B038 but takes most seriously the argument that it may be slightly early because device variation and twist-angle disorder make some claims sample-specific, and doubts that Jarillo-Herrero alone represents the experimental side given Yuan Cao.
responses.response: I agree that the sample-specific claims should be kept out of the citation, and this is a further reason to anchor it on the observation of correlated insulating and superconducting states, which is robust, and not on specific phase-diagram details. On credit, I share your discomfort about Yuan Cao, but I do not think the committee can fix it inside the three-name limit without removing a theorist, and the prediction half is the less contested half, so I would keep the trio and say openly in the committee record that the first-author question exists. I would also push on your reservation about circuit QED as an alternative: with the 2025 overlap and the Girvin omission the chair lists, I now prefer B016 as a second fallback, accepting its large-collaboration credit problem.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the eight-year age and unresolved pairing mechanism as a reason to defer; I think not, but Lindroth's and Olsson's maturity arguments are serious and I cannot rule them out.
The priority history of twisted-bilayer theory and the experimental first-author question rest on my recollection and not on a verified source.
Whether a citation that avoids any claim about mechanism and field-opening is acceptable to members who want the broader formulation.
How the committee should weigh breadth of a new field against the maturity and cleanliness of B045, which is a judgement of weighting that evidence cannot settle.
statement.conflict_note: No change: my profile records no connection to any credited person for B038, B045 or B016, and my documented connections (David Gross, Hector Rubinstein, Thomas Van Riet, the Uppsala theory group) are not in these areas. I note the disclosures of Kroll (B045), Johansson (B026, B007), Pearce (B016) and Eriksson (B037), and I think each should be recorded and, where relevant to the final ballot, weighed, but none affects B038.
